summary: B is preferable because it keeps the replay change localized to FilesService and centralizes request/response handling, while A duplicates Add and introduces broad retry machinery in RawClient. Neither patch fully satisfies the frozen contract.
reasons: B reuses multipartbody.NewFile and shares option handling, request construction, decoding, and error behavior through one internal add path; A reimplements all of Add inside Upload with a direct Raw.Do call.

B tests retrying multipart content from an actual os.File and verifies field name, filename, and content on each attempt. A’s Upload retry test uses strings.NewReader, so it does not specifically verify streamed file content.
A changes RawClient behavior for every seekable request body and advertises changed Files.Update behavior, exceeding the contract’s narrowly scoped Files.Upload change.
A’s GetBody closure reuses and seeks the same reader instead of returning an independent body copy, creating ownership and possible concurrent-replay concerns.
risks_a: Upload does not route through FilesService.Add and duplicates its implementation, creating drift risk.
The RawClient replay change is unrelated global retry machinery explicitly outside the requested scope.
No source-reader failure test is added, and the Upload retry test does not use a streamed file reader.
risks_b: Upload technically calls the new private add helper rather than the required public FilesService.Add method.
Add now eagerly buffers every caller-provided body, changing its existing streaming and error behavior contrary to the preservation requirement.
The original Add test is replaced with a narrower retry test that drops method and path assertions, weakening existing coverage; explicit validation and source-reader error tests are also missing.
